title: Posterior segment ophthalmology clinical trials: Key considerations for retinal study delivery
body_markdown:
Back-of-the-eye, or posterior segment, clinical trials operate within a highly specialized research environment. Programs in wet age-related macular degeneration, diabetic macular edema, geographic atrophy, diabetic retinopathy and inherited retinal disease can involve advanced imaging, complex treatment delivery and participants with meaningful visual impairment. These factors affect nearly every element of ophthalmology study planning, from site selection and recruitment to endpoint governance and retention.


## Begin with the specialist network


Retinal clinical studies frequently require investigators with disease-specific knowledge, advanced imaging infrastructure and hands-on experience with specific treatment regimens. Retina specialists at high-volume practices are often already managing dense clinic schedules that include imaging, injections and, less frequently, laser procedures. Protocols that layer research visits with rigid imaging sequences onto that existing workload, without accounting for real clinic flow, tend to produce slower-than-projected enrollment, higher-than-expected data queries and assessments completed at the edge of the visit window.1


Feasibility assessment should therefore examine imaging capability, treatment experience and daily clinic capacity together, rather than treating them as separate checkboxes.


## Design recruitment around trusted referral pathways, and expect exclusion


Conventional advertising plays a limited role in many retinal studies, where eligibility often depends on detailed imaging findings, treatment history or genetically defined disease subtypes. A retrospective analysis across 87 retinal clinical trials involving 962 patients found that 51.8% were classified as screen failures, with imaging findings and visual acuity criteria the leading causes of exclusion, accounting for 44.5% and 14.7% of failures respectively.2,3


Patient reported barriers add further complexity. In a survey of diabetic retinopathy patients, nearly 30% declined trial participation, and in simulated retinal trial scenarios 45.5% of participants viewed a four-to-five hour visit as too long while 50% viewed a 72-week trial duration as excessive, with anxiety about injections notably higher among those with no prior injection experience.2


These figures suggest that trial recruitment planning for retinal studies should build in realistic screen failure rates from the outset and invest early in relationships with retina specialists and patient advocacy groups who can support identification of eligible and willing participants.


## Protect imaging and visual function endpoints


Posterior segment trials commonly rely on optical coherence tomography, fundus autofluorescence, fundus photography and best corrected visual acuity testing, often reviewed through centralized reading centers to maintain consistency across sites and instrument types. Even well-established metrics carry technical nuance. Published research on diabetic macular edema found that central subfield thickness values are not directly interchangeable across different instruments, requiring validated conversion equations to compare results reliably across a global trial. 4


Masking adds another layer of complexity that is less prominent in anterior segment work. Because treatment effects can sometimes be visible on retinal imaging, masking plans need to map specific risks, such as characteristic treatment related findings on imaging, to specific controls, including separation of treating and assessing personnel, standardized image acquisition and independent central review.5


## Plan around patient and caregiver burden


Retinal trial participants are often older, may have coexisting health conditions and may depend on caregivers for transportation and appointment support. Qualitative research into geographic atrophy found that patients frequently modified daily routines, driving habits and even work schedules because of vision loss, while caregivers reported adjusting their own schedules and experiencing frustration at being unable to improve outcomes for the people they support.6


Broader research into recruiting and retaining older adults across six large multicenter trials identified impaired health status, comorbidities and long study duration as key barriers, and found that solutions such as additional recruitment sites, communication training for site staff, redesigned patient materials and reimbursement of travel costs were the most effective responses.7 These same principles apply directly to retinal studies, where visit frequency and travel demands are often higher than in other ophthalmology research.


## Account for the added complexity of advanced therapies


The operational gap widens further with retinal gene therapies. These programs typically involve a single administration procedure delivered surgically into the eye, followed by long-term safety monitoring that can extend up to 15 years, and they require identifying small, genetically defined and often geographically dispersed patient populations who meet both clinical and genetic criteria.8


## Match the operating model to the study


Retinal trials are not simply anterior segment studies with additional imaging steps. Their success depends on a coordinated system of specialist sites, referral relationships, standardized assessments, central review and thoughtful patient support. Sponsors who build these elements into study design from the outset, rather than adding them after enrollment slows, are better positioned to manage the operational realities of retinal research.
